---
title: "Quiz: texture and co-occurrence matrices"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. GLCMs are symmetric and normalised unless said otherwise.

---

**Q1.** Why can no feature computed from the histogram of an object tell a fine texture from a coarse one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Shuffle the pixels of an object. What happens to its histogram?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The histogram ignores where the values are: shuffling the pixels changes the texture completely but leaves the histogram, and every statistic computed from it (mean, standard deviation, quartiles), unchanged. Texture is about pairs of pixels at some distance, which is what the co-occurrence matrix counts.
:::

---

**Q2.** A GLCM has all its mass on the diagonal. What does that say about the image, and what are its contrast and homogeneity?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The diagonal means $i = j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every pixel has the same (quantised) level as its partner at that offset: the image is constant along that direction, or periodic with the offset as a period. Contrast is 0 and homogeneity is 1.
:::

---

**Q3.** White noise and a smooth texture with the same histogram are measured at $d = 1$ and $d = 10$. Which one's contrast changes between the two distances?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At what distance are the pixels of each texture unrelated?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The smooth texture: at $d = 1$ neighbours are similar (low contrast); at $d = 10$, beyond the grain size, they are unrelated, and the contrast approaches that of white noise. White noise has the same high contrast at every distance, because its pixels are unrelated at any distance.
:::

---

**Q4.** A collaborator quantises each cell to 8 levels between its own minimum and maximum before computing texture. A drug makes the cells dimmer and lowers their contrast. Will the texture features show it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does stretching each cell to its own range do to a dim cell?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Probably not: per-cell min–max quantisation stretches every cell to the full range of 8 levels, which undoes a change in brightness and contrast. Use one fixed range for all cells (and the same $L$), so that a lower contrast shows up as a lower GLCM contrast.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why does $L = 256$ give unreliable texture features on a nucleus of 300 pixels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many cells does the matrix have, and how many pairs are counted?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The matrix has 65 536 cells but only a few hundred pairs are counted: almost every cell is 0 or 1. Features such as entropy and ASM then mostly reflect the number of pairs, and two nuclei with the same texture give quite different values. Use 8–16 levels for small objects.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two programs report "energy" 0.25 and 0.5 for the same matrix. Can both be right?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Naming traps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: some programs call ASM $= \sum p^2$ "energy", others use $\sqrt{\text{ASM}}$. Here ASM = 0.25 and $\sqrt{\text{ASM}} = 0.5$. Always check the formula, not only the name.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is the LBP histogram of an object unchanged when the illumination doubles?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does an LBP code compare?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each bit only records whether a neighbour is at least as bright as the centre. Doubling every value (or adding a constant, or any increasing map) keeps those comparisons, so every code and therefore the histogram stays the same. (Noise in dark, flat regions can still flip bits.)
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that for a symmetric GLCM, contrast $= 2\sigma^2(1 - \text{correlation})$. What is the contrast of a texture with correlation 1? With correlation −1 and $\sigma^2 = 0.25$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand $E[(I - J)^2]$ when $I$ and $J$ have the same mean and variance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$E[(I - J)^2] = \operatorname{var}(I) + \operatorname{var}(J) - 2\operatorname{cov}(I, J) = 2\sigma^2 - 2\rho\sigma^2$ (the means cancel because they are equal). Correlation 1: contrast 0. Correlation −1, $\sigma^2 = 0.25$: contrast 1: the 0/1 checkerboard.
:::
